claim: Mice were trained to categorize visual stimuli as low or high spatial frequencies using a two-alternative forced-choice paradigm.
source: we trained freely-moving mice to categorize visual stimuli as low or high SFs using a two-alternative forced-choice paradigm.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section describing the experimental task design.

claim: The categorical boundary shifted between a lower and a higher spatial frequency several times within a session without a warning cue.
source: Within a session, the categorical boundary shifted between a lower and a higher SF several times without a warning cue (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B showing the task design.

claim: Visual stimuli consisted of 7 spatial frequencies that were logarithmically equally-spaced (0.03, 0.044, 0.065, 0.095, 0.139, 0.204 and 0.3 cycles/°).
source: The visual stimuli consisted of 7 SFs that were logarithmically equally-spaced (0.03, 0.044, 0.065, 0.095, 0.139, 0.204 and 0.3 cycles/o).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Results section describing the visual stimuli.

claim: For the low-boundary block, the optimal decision boundary was located between 0.065 and 0.095 cycles/°.
source: For the low-boundary block, the optimal decision boundary was located between 0.065 and 0.095 cycles/o, and gratings at 0.03 and 0.095 cycles/o (SF1 and SF4 in Figure 1B) were frequently presented in 90% of trials.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: For the high-boundary block, the optimal decision boundary was located between 0.095 and 0.139 cycles/°.
source: For the high-boundary block, the optimal decision boundary was located between 0.095 and 0.139 cycles/o, and gratings at 0.095 and 0.3 cycles/o (SF4 and SF7 in Figure 1B) were frequently presented in 90% of trials.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The stimulus statistics differed between the low-boundary and high-boundary blocks.
source: As a result, the stimulus statistics differed between the low-boundary and high-boundary blocks.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a consequence of the different stimulus presentation frequencies in the two block types.

claim: The number of trials in each block was 61.9 ± 0.33 (mean ± SEM) across all sessions from 10 mice.
source: Across all sessions from 10 mice (11 sessions/mouse), the number of trials in each block was 61.9 ± 0.33 (mean ± SEM) and the number of switches in a session was 6.91 ± 0.29 (mean ± SEM) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The number of switches in a session was 6.91 ± 0.29 (mean ± SEM) across all sessions from 10 mice.
source: Across all sessions from 10 mice (11 sessions/mouse), the number of trials in each block was 61.9 ± 0.33 (mean ± SEM) and the number of switches in a session was 6.91 ± 0.29 (mean ± SEM) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The subjective categorical boundary estimated from the psychometric curve was significantly lower in the low-boundary than in the high-boundary block (p=2 × 10−3, n = 10 mice).
source: The subjective categorical boundary estimated from the psychometric curve was significantly lower in the low-boundary than in the high-boundary block (p=2 × 10−3, n = 10 mice, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 1H), suggesting that the mice adapted their DC to the boundary contingency.
evidence: This is stated in the text with statistical test results and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Mice adapted their decision criterion to the boundary contingency.
source: The subjective categorical boundary estimated from the psychometric curve was significantly lower in the low-boundary than in the high-boundary block (p=2 × 10−3, n = 10 mice, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 1H), suggesting that the mice adapted their DC to the boundary contingency.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the significant difference in subjective boundaries between blocks.

claim: The number of trials to reverse choice was 6.41 ± 0.42 (mean ± SEM, n = 10 mice).
source: The number of trials to reverse choice, which was the number of trials needed to cross the 50% correct rate of the fitted curve, was 6.41 ± 0.42 (mean ± SEM, n = 10 mice, Figure 1J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The last 15 trials before boundary switch were defined as the stable period.
source: In the following analysis, we defined the last 15 trials before boundary switch as the stable period, and the first 15 trials after boundary switch as the switching period.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a definition for subsequent analyses.

claim: The first 15 trials after boundary switch were defined as the switching period.
source: In the following analysis, we defined the last 15 trials before boundary switch as the stable period, and the first 15 trials after boundary switch as the switching period.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a definition for subsequent analyses.

claim: A logistic regression model with a dynamic decision criterion was designed to fit the mouse's choice on each trial.
source: To examine the behavioral strategies of mice in trials before and after the boundary switch, we designed a logistic regression model with a dynamic DC to fit the mouse's choice on each trial.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the computational modeling approach.

claim: In the dynamic decision criterion model, the probability of choosing right in current trial is a logistic function of a decision variable z.
source: In this model, the probability p of choosing right in current trial t is a logistic function of a decision variable z, which is the difference between the stimulus S weighted by γ1 (γ1 > 0) and the subjective DC of the animal (Figure 2A, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The decision criterion is updated on a trial-by-trial basis according to choice outcome and sensory history.
source: The DC is updated on a trial-by-trial basis according to choice outcome and sensory history (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: For both the stable and switching periods, γ1 was significantly larger than zero (p=2 × 10−3, n = 10).
source: For both the stable and switching periods, γ1 was significantly larger than zero (p=2 × 10−3, n = 10, Wilcoxon signed rank test), indicating that current sensory information was used to form decision and guide action selection in both periods.
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results.

claim: Current sensory information was used to form decision and guide action selection in both the stable and switching periods.
source: For both the stable and switching periods, γ1 was significantly larger than zero (p=2 × 10−3, n = 10, Wilcoxon signed rank test), indicating that current sensory information was used to form decision and guide action selection in both periods.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the significant γ1 parameter.

claim: The reward history parameter α1 was not significantly different from zero in either the stable (p=0.23) or the switching period (p=0.49).
source: The reward history parameter α1 was not significantly different from zero in either the stable (p=0.23) or the switching period (p=0.49, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results.

claim: The non-reward history parameter α2 was significantly larger than zero in the stable period (p=9.8 × 10−3).
source: The non-reward history parameter α2 was significantly larger than zero in the stable period (p=9.8 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed rank test), but not significantly different from zero in the switching period (p=0.7, Wilcoxon signed rank test), suggesting that the mice adopted a lose-shift strategy only in the stable period.
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results.

claim: The non-reward history parameter α2 was not significantly different from zero in the switching period (p=0.7).
source: The non-reward history parameter α2 was significantly larger than zero in the stable period (p=9.8 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed rank test), but not significantly different from zero in the switching period (p=0.7, Wilcoxon signed rank test), suggesting that the mice adopted a lose-shift strategy only in the stable period.
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results.

claim: Mice adopted a lose-shift strategy only in the stable period.
source: The non-reward history parameter α2 was significantly larger than zero in the stable period (p=9.8 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed rank test), but not significantly different from zero in the switching period (p=0.7, Wilcoxon signed rank test), suggesting that the mice adopted a lose-shift strategy only in the stable period.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the α2 parameter values.

claim: The sensory history parameter γ2 was significantly larger than zero in both the stable and the switching periods (p=0.037 and p=2 × 10−3).
source: The sensory history parameter γ2 was significantly larger than zero in both the stable and the switching periods (p=0.037 and p=2 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed rank test), suggesting that the mice could optimally use the sensory history of non-reversing stimuli to guide choice in both periods.
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results.

claim: Mice could optimally use the sensory history of non-reversing stimuli to guide choice in both the stable and switching periods.
source: The sensory history parameter γ2 was significantly larger than zero in both the stable and the switching periods (p=0.037 and p=2 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed rank test), suggesting that the mice could optimally use the sensory history of non-reversing stimuli to guide choice in both periods.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the γ2 parameter values.

claim: The DC-drift parameter β was significantly larger than zero in the switching period (p=2 × 10−3) but not in the stable period (p=0.56).
source: The DC-drift parameter β was significantly larger than zero in the switching period (p=2 × 10−3) but not in the stable period (p=0.56, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results.

claim: The decision criterion tended to drift towards zero in the switching period, reflecting the tendency of mice to abandon previous decision criterion.
source: This demonstrates that the DC tended to drift towards zero in the switching period, reflecting the tendency of mice to abandon pervious decision criterion.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the β parameter value in the switching period.

claim: For the stable period, only model 6 (γ1 = 1) showed a significantly lower cross-validated likelihood compared to the full model (p=2 × 10−3).
source: For the stable period, only model 6 (γ1 = 1) showed a significantly lower cross-validated (CV) likelihood as compared to that of the full model (p=2 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 3A), indicating that γ1 (weight of current stimulus) was most important for predicting choices during steady state of stimulus-action association.
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: γ1 (weight of current stimulus) was most important for predicting choices during steady state of stimulus-action association.
source: For the stable period, only model 6 (γ1 = 1) showed a significantly lower cross-validated (CV) likelihood as compared to that of the full model (p=2 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 3A), indicating that γ1 (weight of current stimulus) was most important for predicting choices during steady state of stimulus-action association.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the model comparison results.

claim: For the switching period, the CV likelihood for model 5 (β = 0), model 6 (γ1 = 1) and model 7 (γ2 = 0) was significantly reduced compared to the full model (p=5.9 × 10−3, 2 × 10−3 and 5.9 × 10−3).
source: For the switching period, the CV likelihood for model 5 (β = 0), model 6 (γ1 = 1) and model 7 (γ2 = 0) was significantly reduced as compared to that of the full model (p=5.9 × 10−3, 2 × 10−3 and 5.9 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 3B), demonstrating that β, γ1 and γ2 were important parameters for explaining choices in the switching phase.
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: β, γ1 and γ2 were important parameters for explaining choices in the switching phase.
source: For the switching period, the CV likelihood for model 5 (β = 0), model 6 (γ1 = 1) and model 7 (γ2 = 0) was significantly reduced as compared to that of the full model (p=5.9 × 10−3, 2 × 10−3 and 5.9 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 3B), demonstrating that β, γ1 and γ2 were important parameters for explaining choices in the switching phase.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the model comparison results.

claim: For both the stable and switching periods, the CV likelihood for model 4 (α1 = 0 and α2 = 0) was significantly higher than that of the full model (p=0.037 and 0.02).
source: For both the stable and switching periods, the CV likelihood for model 4 (α1 = 0 and α2 = 0) was significantly higher than that of the full model (p=0.037 and 0.02, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 3A and B), suggesting that choice outcome was not useful to guide the mice's choice.
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Choice outcome was not useful to guide the mice's choice.
source: For both the stable and switching periods, the CV likelihood for model 4 (α1 = 0 and α2 = 0) was significantly higher than that of the full model (p=0.037 and 0.02, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 3A and B), suggesting that choice outcome was not useful to guide the mice's choice.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the model comparison results.

claim: The CV likelihood of the RL model was significantly lower than that of the best dynamic-DC model (model 4) in the switching period (p=2 × 10−3).
source: We found that the CV likelihood of the RL model was significantly lower than that of the best dynamic-DC model (model 4: α1 = 0 and α2 = 0) in the switching period (p=2 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 3F), indicating that the behavioral strategy in the switching period was better accounted for by the model with a dynamic decision criterion.
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The behavioral strategy in the switching period was better accounted for by the model with a dynamic decision criterion than by the RL model.
source: We found that the CV likelihood of the RL model was significantly lower than that of the best dynamic-DC model (model 4: α1 = 0 and α2 = 0) in the switching period (p=2 × 10−3, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 3F), indicating that the behavioral strategy in the switching period was better accounted for by the model with a dynamic decision criterion.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the model comparison results.

claim: Model 4 of the dynamic-DC model (α1 = 0 and α2 = 0) was the best model for the greatest number of mice in both the stable and the switching periods.
source: We found that model 4 of the dynamic-DC model (α1 = 0 and α2 = 0) was the best model for the greatest number of mice in both the stable and the switching periods (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: Larger value of γ2 in the switching period (model 4) was associated with fewer number of trials to reverse choice (Pearson's r = −0.71, p=0.02).
source: In addition, larger value of γ2 in the switching period (model 4) was associated with fewer number of trials to reverse choice (Pearson's r = −0.71, p=0.02, Figure 3K).
evidence: This is stated with correlation statistics and shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The sensory history of non-reversing stimuli, rather than the choice-outcome history of reversing stimulus, was important for correct adaptation of decision boundary in this task.
source: Taken together, the above results suggest that the sensory history of non-reversing stimuli, rather than the choice-outcome history of reversing stimulus, was important for correct adaptation of decision boundary in this task.
evidence: This is stated as a summary interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: AAV2/9-hSyn-hM4D-mCitrine was bilaterally injected in M2 to express the Gi-protein-coupled receptor hM4D.
source: We bilaterally injected AAV2/9-hSyn-hM4D-mCitrine in M2 to express the Gi-protein-coupled receptor hM4D (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) significantly reduced the firing rates of M2 neurons (p<0.001, n = 24 and 14 cells from two mice).
source: Electrophysiological recordings validated that intraperitoneal injection of clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) could significantly reduce the firing rates of M2 neurons (p<0.001, n = 24 and 14 cells from two mice, respectively, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Chemogenetic inactivation of M2 significantly decreased the correct rate for the reversing stimulus during the switching period (p=0.022).
source: We found that chemogenetic inactivation of M2 significantly decreased the correct rate and response latency for the reversing stimulus during the switching period (p=0.022 and 0.019, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA followed by Sidak's multiple comparisons test), while did not significantly affect those during the stable period (p=0.87 and 0.47, n = 10, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA followed by Sidak's multiple comparisons test, Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Chemogenetic inactivation of M2 significantly decreased the response latency for the reversing stimulus during the switching period (p=0.019).
source: We found that chemogenetic inactivation of M2 significantly decreased the correct rate and response latency for the reversing stimulus during the switching period (p=0.022 and 0.019, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA followed by Sidak's multiple comparisons test), while did not significantly affect those during the stable period (p=0.87 and 0.47, n = 10, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA followed by Sidak's multiple comparisons test, Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Chemogenetic inactivation of M2 did not significantly affect the correct rate or response latency for the reversing stimulus during the stable period (p=0.87 and 0.47).
source: We found that chemogenetic inactivation of M2 significantly decreased the correct rate and response latency for the reversing stimulus during the switching period (p=0.022 and 0.019, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA followed by Sidak's multiple comparisons test), while did not significantly affect those during the stable period (p=0.87 and 0.47, n = 10, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA followed by Sidak's multiple comparisons test, Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: After the boundary switch, the number of trials to reverse choice for the reversing stimulus was greater in the CNO sessions (7.48 ± 1.19) than in the saline sessions (5.45 ± 0.40, p=0.049, n = 10).
source: After the boundary switch, the number of trials to reverse choice for the reversing stimulus was greater in the CNO sessions (7.48 ± 1.19, mean ± SEM) than in the saline sessions (5.45 ± 0.40, mean ± SEM, p=0.049, n = 10, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results.

claim: M2 inactivation did not affect the correct rate for the non-reversing stimuli, the number of trials within a block, the number of switches per session or the distance between the two subjective categorical boundaries.
source: On the other hand, M2 inactivation did not affect the correct rate for the non-reversing stimuli, the number of trials within a block, the number of switches per session or the distance between the two subjective categorical boundaries estimated from trials after the switching period (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that M2 inactivation did not cause general deficit in motor control or visual perception.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: M2 inactivation did not cause general deficit in motor control or visual perception.
source: On the other hand, M2 inactivation did not affect the correct rate for the non-reversing stimuli, the number of trials within a block, the number of switches per session or the distance between the two subjective categorical boundaries estimated from trials after the switching period (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that M2 inactivation did not cause general deficit in motor control or visual perception.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the lack of effects on various behavioral measures.

claim: Bilateral M2 inactivation impaired adaptive action selection for the reversing stimulus specifically during the switching period when the mice needed to remap the stimulus-action association.
source: Thus, bilateral M2 inactivation impaired adaptive action selection for the reversing stimulus specifically during the switching period when the mice needed to remap the stimulus-action association.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the M2 inactivation effects.

claim: M2 inactivation did not cause significant changes in the model parameters or in the DC curves during the stable period (p>0.05).
source: We found that M2 inactivation did not cause significant changes in the model parameters (p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test) or in the DC curves (p>0.05, two-way repeated measures ANOVA) during the stable period (Figure 4E and G), and did not significantly affect the value of γ1 (weight of current stimulus) in either the stable or the switching period (p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figures 4E and 4G.

claim: M2 inactivation did not significantly affect the value of γ1 (weight of current stimulus) in either the stable or the switching period (p>0.05).
source: We found that M2 inactivation did not cause significant changes in the model parameters (p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test) or in the DC curves (p>0.05, two-way repeated measures ANOVA) during the stable period (Figure 4E and G), and did not significantly affect the value of γ1 (weight of current stimulus) in either the stable or the switching period (p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results.

claim: M2 inactivation caused a significant decrease in γ2 in both model 1 and model four during the switching period (p=0.02 and 0.014).
source: By contrast, M2 inactivation caused a significant decrease in γ2 in both model 1 and model four during the switching period (p=0.02 and 0.014, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 4F), suggesting an impairment in utilizing sensory history of the non-reversing stimuli to update DC.
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: M2 inactivation caused an impairment in utilizing sensory history of the non-reversing stimuli to update decision criterion.
source: By contrast, M2 inactivation caused a significant decrease in γ2 in both model 1 and model four during the switching period (p=0.02 and 0.014, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 4F), suggesting an impairment in utilizing sensory history of the non-reversing stimuli to update DC.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the decrease in γ2.

claim: M2 inactivation slowed down the change of decision criterion during the switching period.
source: M2 inactivation also slowed down the change of DC during the switching period (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: A major effect of bilateral M2 inactivation was an impairment in updating internal decision criterion according to the sensory history of non-reversing stimuli during the switching period.
source: Thus, a major effect of bilateral M2 inactivation was an impairment in updating internal decision criterion according to the sensory history of non-reversing stimuli during the switching period.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the M2 inactivation effects on model parameters.

claim: Bilateral inactivation of mPFC or OFC did not cause significant change in the performance for the reversing stimulus, the distance between internal categorical boundaries or number of switches per session (p>0.05).
source: We found that bilateral inactivation of mPFC or OFC did not cause significant change in the performance for the reversing stimulus, the distance between internal categorical boundaries or number of switches per session (p>0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test, mPFC: n = 13 mice, OFC: n = 9 mice, Figure 4—figure supplement 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 7), although OFC inactivation tended to increase the number of trials per block (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 6 and 7.

claim: Inactivation of mPFC or OFC did not affect the parameters in the dynamic-DC model.
source: Inactivation of mPFC or OFC did not affect the parameters in the dynamic-DC model (Figure 4—figure supplement 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 6 and 7.

claim: The impaired performance for the reversing stimulus during the switching period was specific to M2 inactivation.
source: Thus, the impaired performance for the reversing stimulus during the switching period was specific to M2 inactivation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the comparison of M2, mPFC, and OFC inactivation effects.

claim: The choice preferences in correct and wrong trials were positively correlated (stable period: Pearson's r = 0.36, p=1.0 × 10−4; switching period: Pearson's r = 0.24, p=9.3 × 10−3; n = 113).
source: We found that the choice preferences in correct and wrong trials were positively correlated (stable period: Pearson's r = 0.36, p=1.0 × 10−4; switching period: Pearson's r = 0.24, p=9.3 × 10−3; n = 113, Figure 5K), indicating that M2 activity during stimulus-viewing period reflects the orienting choice of the mice, consistent with the previous report (Erlich et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with correlation statistics and shown in Figure 5K.

claim: M2 activity during stimulus-viewing period reflects the orienting choice of the mice.
source: We found that the choice preferences in correct and wrong trials were positively correlated (stable period: Pearson's r = 0.36, p=1.0 × 10−4; switching period: Pearson's r = 0.24, p=9.3 × 10−3; n = 113, Figure 5K), indicating that M2 activity during stimulus-viewing period reflects the orienting choice of the mice, consistent with the previous report (Erlich et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the correlation between choice preferences in correct and wrong trials, and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: For correct trials, the preference for left-right choice in current trial showed a significant negative correlation with the preference for stimulus in the last trial (stable period: Pearson's r = −0.87, p=3.2 × 10−23; switching period: Pearson's r = −0.92, p=9.5 × 10−31; n = 72).
source: For correct trials, the preference for left-right choice in current trial showed a significant negative correlation with the preference for stimulus in the last trial (stable period: Pearson's r = −0.87, p=3.2 × 10−23; switching period: Pearson's r = −0.92, p=9.5 × 10−31; n = 72, Figure 5L), and such effect could be observed for M2 neurons recorded in both hemispheres (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated with correlation statistics and shown in Figure 5L.

claim: The choice preference of M2 neurons is strongly influenced by stimulus history, and the preference for choice in current trial is coupled to the preference for stimulus in the last but not earlier trial.
source: Thus, the result suggests that the choice preference of M2 neurons is strongly influenced by stimulus history, and the preference for choice in current trial is coupled to the preference for stimulus in the last but not earlier trial.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the correlation analysis results.

claim: For wrong trials, the correlation between choice preference and previous-stimulus preference was not significant (stable period: Pearson's r = −0.15, p=0.2; switching period: Pearson's r = 0.08, p=0.5; n = 72).
source: For wrong trials, however, the correlation between choice preference and previous-stimulus preference was not significant (stable period: Pearson's r = −0.15, p=0.2; switching period: Pearson's r = 0.08, p=0.5; n = 72, Figure 5M).
evidence: This is stated with correlation statistics and shown in Figure 5M.

claim: The left-right choice preference of M2 neurons was intimately related to the preference for previous stimulus in correct trials.
source: Thus, the left-right choice preference of M2 neurons was intimately related to the preference for previous stimulus in correct trials, consistent with the finding that sensory history of previous non-reversing stimuli was important for correct action selection in the task.
evidence: This is stated as a summary interpretation of the correlation analysis results.

claim: The accuracy of predicting choice was significantly higher in the switching than in the stable period for correct trials (p<1.0 × 10−4).
source: As shown by Figure 6A, the accuracy of predicting choice was significantly higher in the switching than in the stable period for correct trials (p<1.0 × 10−4, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For both the stable and switching periods, the accuracy of predicting choice was higher for correct trials than for wrong trials (p<1.0 × 10−4).
source: For both the stable and switching periods, the accuracy of predicting choice was higher for correct trials than for wrong trials (p<1.0 × 10−4, Wilcoxon rank sum test, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The accuracy for classifying the previous stimulus was significantly higher in the switching than in the stable period for correct trials (p<1.0 × 10−4).
source: When we examined the accuracy for classifying the previous stimulus as a lower or a higher frequency, we also found that the accuracy was significantly higher in the switching than in the stable period for correct trials (p<1.0 × 10−4, Wilcoxon rank sum test), and the accuracy for the switching period was higher in correct than in wrong trials (p<1.0 × 10−4, Wilcoxon rank sum test, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The accuracy for classifying the previous stimulus in the switching period was higher in correct than in wrong trials (p<1.0 × 10−4).
source: When we examined the accuracy for classifying the previous stimulus as a lower or a higher frequency, we also found that the accuracy was significantly higher in the switching than in the stable period for correct trials (p<1.0 × 10−4, Wilcoxon rank sum test), and the accuracy for the switching period was higher in correct than in wrong trials (p<1.0 × 10−4, Wilcoxon rank sum test, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Representations of upcoming choice and sensory history in M2 were stronger during the switching period than during the stable period.
source: Thus, the results demonstrate that representations of upcoming choice and sensory history in M2 were stronger during the switching period, when mice were faced with a demand to switch stimulus-action association, than during the stable period.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the decoding accuracy results.

claim: The stronger representations of upcoming choice and sensory history in M2 during the switching period correspond with the causal contribution of M2 in controlling action selection when the stimulus-action association was remapped.
source: Thus, the results demonstrate that representations of upcoming choice and sensory history in M2 were stronger during the switching period, when mice were faced with a demand to switch stimulus-action association, than during the stable period. This corresponds with the causal contribution of M2 in controlling action selection when the stimulus-action association was remapped.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation linking the neural representation results to the causal manipulation results.

claim: M2 causally contributes to flexible action selection during stimulus categorization.
source: Thus, M2 causally contributes to flexible action selection during stimulus categorization, with the representations of upcoming choice and sensory history regulated by the demand to remap stimulus-action association.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The representations of upcoming choice and sensory history in M2 are regulated by the demand to remap stimulus-action association.
source: Thus, M2 causally contributes to flexible action selection during stimulus categorization, with the representations of upcoming choice and sensory history regulated by the demand to remap stimulus-action association.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Mice depended on sensory history to correctly change stimulus-action association when categorical boundary switched between blocks of trials.
source: Using behavioral modeling to analyze choices in a flexible visual categorization task, we found that mice depended on sensory history to correctly change stimulus-action association when categorical boundary switched between blocks of trials.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the behavioral modeling findings.

claim: M2 activity was specifically required for correct choices during remapping of stimulus-action association, but not when the sensorimotor association was stable.
source: Chemogenetic manipulation showed that M2 activity was specifically required for correct choices during remapping of stimulus-action association, but not when the sensorimotor association was stable.
